I’ve been farming these 65 mu in Quzhou for 25 years, and I know every patch of soil like the back of my hand. I’m 59 now, and with just three of us in the household, I have to be smart about labor and costs. The wheat-maize double crop is my bread and butter—it’s reliable and the county grain station buys it without hassle. I’ll keep 45 mu in that rotation. I use improved wheat seed because it sprouts well through our Hebei winters, and hybrid maize seed because nothing else gives me the density and yield I need in the short summer window after wheat harvest. For the maize, I won’t till much after combining the wheat—there’s no time, and no-till saves moisture and diesel.

The other 20 mu I split into cash crops. Watermelon brings the best money per mu if the price holds, so I’ll put 8 mu into melons in spring. They need heavy potassium and careful watering, but I’ve got the well. After the melons come off in mid-summer, I’ll follow with 6 mu of autumn cabbage on that same ground or the adjacent plot—cabbage grows fast and the market in Handan is steady. I’ll keep 4 mu of chili through summer; it needs more pesticide sprays for mites and aphids, but the dried chili price is usually good by New Year. I’ve also got 2 mu of stevia that a buyer from Shandong promised to purchase—low hassle, and I can manage it with the family labor. 

I don’t over-fertilize anymore. The soil here has some base fertility, so I cut back slightly on nitrogen to save cost and keep the groundwater a bit cleaner. Well irrigation means I can water when I need to, but pumping costs electricity, so I water at the critical stages only: jointing and heading for wheat, grain-filling for maize, and flowering/fruiting for the vegetables. I use rotary tillage for everything except the maize, where I drill straight into the wheat stubble. I expect my wheat to hit around 490 kg/mu and maize about 570 kg/mu if the summer storms don’t flatten them.
